analysis.one_liner: Restores coastal wetlands that store carbon, bans most new offshore oil drilling, sets offshore wind leasing targets, and taxes new plastic.
analysis.headline: The House Natural Resources Committee approved the bill 23–19 in July 2021, but it was only reported to the House floor calendar on December 30, 2022 — two days before the Congress ended — and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed NOAA to run a 'blue carbon' program that would map, protect, and restore coastal wetlands, seagrass, and kelp forests that pull carbon out of the air, with grants prioritizing low-income, Tribal, and rural coastal communities. It would have banned new offshore oil and gas leasing almost everywhere except the Central and Western Gulf of Mexico, set deadlines for leasing enough offshore wind for 30 gigawatts of power by 2030, created a tax on new (virgin) plastic, and added climate-adaptation programs for fisheries, coastal towns, U.S. territories, and marine mammal protection. The House Natural Resources Committee approved it on a 23–19 vote in July 2021, but the bill was only formally reported to the full House on December 30, 2022, and the 117th Congress ended two days later without any floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities — especially low-income communities, communities of color, and Tribal and Indigenous communities, which the grant programs explicitly prioritize — gain flood protection, restored wetlands, and resilience funding. U.S. territories gain climate research, disaster cost-share waivers, and Runit Dome monitoring. Fishing communities gain climate-adapted management and fuel-efficiency grants, and offshore wind developers and workers gain guaranteed lease targets. The offshore oil and gas industry is the clearest loser, barred from new leasing outside the Central and Western Gulf of Mexico; virgin plastic producers face a new excise tax.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities and offshore wind developers

how_it_helps.text: Directs NOAA to run a Blue Carbon Program and a competitive grant program (authorized at $300 million per year for fiscal 2022–2026) to protect and restore 1.5 million acres of coastal wetlands, seagrass, and kelp over ten years, with priority for projects benefiting communities of color, low-income communities, Tribal and Indigenous communities, and rural communities.

Prohibits new offshore oil and gas leasing and seismic exploration permits everywhere on the Outer Continental Shelf except the Central and Western Gulf of Mexico, and requires the best available noise-reducing technology for exploration.

Sets binding targets for the Interior Department to lease at least 12.5 gigawatts of offshore wind by 2025 and 30 gigawatts by 2030, and directs that 30% of offshore wind lease revenue go into the National Oceans and Coastal Security Fund.
Amends the Coastal Barrier Resources Act so prospective buyers are told when property sits in the Coastal Barrier Resources System, where federal flood insurance and other subsidies are limited.

Establishes a climate and fisheries research and management program, grants for fuel-efficient fishing vessels, promotion of American-caught seafood for federal purchases, and negotiating objectives to eliminate fish subsidies that drive overfishing in trade agreements.

Provides coastal resilience grants (living shorelines, working waterfronts), insular-area programs including monitoring of the Runit Dome nuclear waste site and waivers of non-federal cost shares for climate and disaster projects in the territories, Tribal resilience grants through the Bureau of Indian Affairs, and protections for marine mammals including vessel speed and noise measures.
Creates a virgin plastic excise tax with proceeds to a Virgin Plastic Trust Fund, and directs measures to cut greenhouse gas emissions from shipping vessels.

analysis.who_pays: The offshore oil and gas industry loses access to nearly all new federal waters; virgin plastic producers pay a new excise tax, part of which would likely reach consumers through prices; shipping and fishing operators bear new vessel, noise, and habitat-protection requirements; and the federal treasury would fund roughly $2 billion a year in authorized programs for fiscal 2022–2026.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore drillers and virgin plastic makers

drawbacks.text: The bill bans new offshore oil and gas leasing nearly everywhere except the Central and Western Gulf of Mexico, which could reduce future domestic oil and gas supply and put upward pressure on energy prices or increase reliance on imports.
Title XIII creates a virgin plastic excise tax, and excise taxes on producers are typically passed at least partly to consumers through higher prices on plastic goods and packaging.

The bill authorizes billions of dollars in new spending for fiscal years 2022 through 2026, including $300 million per year for blue carbon grants and $200 million per year each to three land agencies for restoration, adding to federal outlays.

The blue carbon 'areas of significance' rules would require federal agencies to avoid, mitigate, or offset any action harming designated areas, and the strengthened essential fish habitat consultation requirements would apply to federally authorized projects — safeguards that could also slow or add costs to infrastructure, coastal construction, and other development.

Several marine mammal provisions, including vessel restrictions in marine mammal habitat and speed-related measures, impose operating constraints and costs on the shipping, fishing, and port industries.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver real, durable benefits — coastal flood protection, restored wetlands, climate-adapted fisheries, and clean power — while the costs fall mostly on industries whose products drive the problems the bill targets: offshore oil and gas, virgin plastic makers, and shipping. The strongest good-faith objections are that the offshore leasing ban could tighten domestic oil supply and that the plastic tax would be partly passed to consumers, though both are deliberate attempts to price environmental harm that the public currently pays for in other ways (spills, pollution, flood losses). The heaviest criticism of the bill as legislation is design: billions in authorizations across a dozen titles, many studies and interagency processes, and new consultation requirements that could slow federal projects. It is an ambitious bill with real costs, but its costs are aimed at concentrated interests and its benefits broadly shared.

outcome.mechanism: The Natural Resources Committee approved it 23–19, but it sat for a year and a half, was finally reported to the House floor calendar with two days left in the Congress, and died without a vote when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 8, 2021, by Rep. Raúl Grijalva and referred to seven committees, with Natural Resources taking the lead.
On July 14, 2021, the Natural Resources Committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 23 to 19.

The committee then took nearly eighteen months to formally report the bill; on December 30, 2022, it was reported as amended with House Report 117-695, the six other committees were discharged, and it was placed on the Union Calendar.
No floor vote ever followed; the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and all pending bills died.

The reported version would have banned most new offshore oil and gas leasing outside the Central and Western Gulf of Mexico, set offshore wind lease targets, created blue carbon restoration grant programs, added a virgin plastic excise tax, and expanded coastal resilience and fisheries programs.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The offshore oil and gas industry, which would have faced a near-total ban on new federal leases, and virgin plastic producers, which would have faced a new excise tax, are better off because the bill died. House Democratic leadership also avoided forcing members to take votes on drilling and plastic taxes in the final days of the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil and virgin plastic producers

sides.party_line_note: Every cosponsor was a Democrat, and the committee's 23–19 vote to report the bill broke down along party lines, with the Democratic majority supplying the 23 yes votes.

industries.note: The bill prohibits new oil and gas leases and new seismic exploration permits on nearly all of the Outer Continental Shelf, sparing only the Central and Western Gulf of Mexico, and requires best-available noise-reducing technology for exploration. The industry loses future access to federal waters and the revenue that comes with it; the public gains reduced spill and climate risk.

The bill sets mandatory lease targets of 12.5 GW by 2025 and 30 GW by 2030, eases data sharing for siting, funds research on wind-wildlife interactions, extends industry collaboration authority, and routes 30% of wind lease revenue to coastal security funding. Wind developers gain a guaranteed leasing pipeline; the public gains clean power, though the industry becomes the designated channel for offshore energy.

A new excise tax on virgin plastic would raise costs for plastic resin producers and their customers, with proceeds funding a Virgin Plastic Trust Fund. Producers' interest runs against the bill's pollution-reduction goal; some of the tax would likely reach consumers through prices.

Fishers gain climate-adapted management, fuel-efficiency retrofits, and promotion of American-caught seafood for federal buyers, but bear new vessel restrictions and noise and speed measures to protect marine mammals, stricter essential fish habitat consultation, and negotiating objectives against capacity-expanding fish subsidies. Most provisions support the long-term health of the resource fishers depend on.

The bill directs measures to cut greenhouse gas emissions from shipping and funds speed-reduction and quieting awards and port grants to reduce harm to whales, adding compliance costs while offering grants and a healthier marine environment.

The bill studies expanding the Coastal Barrier Resources System to the Pacific coast and requires disclosure to buyers that property is in the system, where federal flood insurance and development subsidies are limited — modest constraints on building in high-risk coastal areas.
